docs.text: • https://www.mirantis.com/cloud-native-concepts/getting-started-with-kubernetes/what-are-kubernetes-secrets/

docs.title: Longhorn
docs.text: Longhorn provides the distributed block storage layer for this cluster. The Helm release, default settings, and supporting resources are managed declaratively in apps/longhorn/kustomization.yaml, so all configuration changes should flow through GitOps.

docs.title: Accessing the Longhorn UI
docs.text:
• Dashboard: https://storage.internal.neese-web.de (published through Traefik with Authelia forward-auth).
  • In-cluster service: http://longhorn-frontend.longhorn.svc.cluster.local.
  • Use the UI for day-to-day administration (volume health, replicas, backups, recurring jobs) and to confirm Git-driven changes after syncs.

docs.title: Default Storage Classes and PVC Usage
docs.text:
• The longhorn StorageClass is marked as the default via a sync-time patch, so workloads can omit storageClassName unless an alternative is required.
  • The reclaim policy is set to Retain. PVCs and underlying volumes are kept after a workload is deleted to prevent accidental data loss; clean up volumes explicitly in the UI or via kubectl delete volume.longhorn.io/<name>.
  • Typical PVC:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: example-longhorn-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  storageClassName: longhorn
  • Validate provisioning with kubectl get pvc and kubectl get volumes.longhorn.io -n longhorn.

docs.title: Backups, Snapshots, and Automation
docs.text:
• Longhorn's own backup target is disabled (defaultBackupStore.backupTarget: "" in apps/longhorn/kustomization.yaml). Volume data is backed up by the restic backup fleet instead (see Backup). The former Wasabi target's credentials were revoked, and with a dead S3 target longhorn-manager re-ran longhorn backup ls in a tight loop at 100-200% CPU.
  • To re-enable it, set defaultBackupStore.backupTarget and backupTargetCredentialSecret to a reachable target and a valid secret. Since chart 1.8 these keys live under defaultBackupStore; defaultSettings.backupTarget is ignored.
  • There is no CSI VolumeSnapshotClass for Longhorn backups (the former longhorn-vsc-backup, type: bak, was removed together with the revoked wasabi-secret). Re-add one alongside a working backup target if CSI-driven backups are needed again.
  • A recurring job named trim-filesystem runs daily at 06:00 to perform filesystem trim on all volumes assigned to the default group. Adjust or add jobs through Git in apps/longhorn/longhorn-config.enc.yaml.

docs.title: Operational Guidance
docs.text:
• Follow the controlled upgrade/maintenance steps captured in docs/operations/longhorn-maintenance.md when performing Longhorn upgrades or disruptive changes.
  • Monitor Longhorn health dashboards exposed through Grafana (PVC longhorn-pvc-grafana) to detect replica rebuilds or disk pressure early.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Volume still attached to a node: Longhorn enforces exclusive attachment. If a pod restart reports Volume is already exclusively attached to one node, wait for the detachment timeout or force detach the volume (UI → Volume → Detach), ensuring the old workload is fully terminated first.
  • Replica rebuild loops: Check node disk usage and engine replica logs in the UI; if disk capacity is low, cordon the node, migrate workloads, and expand storage.
  • Backup target errors / high longhorn-manager CPU: Check kubectl get backuptargets.longhorn.io -n longhorn default -o yaml. An unreachable or unauthorized target makes longhorn-manager retry longhorn backup ls several times per second; fix the credentials or clear the target.

docs.title: td-sync
docs.text:
td is a task-tracker CLI with an optional sync server so multiple machines (or AI sessions) can share the same issue database. td-sync is that sync server, deployed in this cluster.

  • Namespace: td-sync
  • URL: https://td.internal.neese-web.de
  • ArgoCD app: 62-td-sync
  • Image: built by madic/docker-td on forge.geekbundle.org, pinned by tag and digest in apps/td-sync/k8s.td-sync.yaml

docs.title: Creating a user
docs.text: Upstream's device-login flow (td auth login) cannot create the first account: unknown emails are silently accepted and suppressed for enumeration protection, so nothing actually gets created. SYNC_ALLOW_SIGNUP is not consulted by that endpoint at all, and stays "false" in this deployment.

docs.title: The admin CLI does not work in this deployment
docs.text:
td-sync admin create-user is upstream's provisioning command, but it cannot run here:

$ kubectl exec -n td-sync deploy/td-sync -- td-sync admin create-user --email <address>
error: open database: open database: set journal mode: database is locked (5) (SQLITE_BUSY)

The command opens the database and sets journal_mode, which needs an exclusive lock. Litestream — which the entrypoint wraps the server in — holds a long-running read transaction to stop WAL checkpoints, so that lock never becomes free. Upstream's note that the command should run "while the server is NOT holding the DB open" is therefore not advisory here but absolute: it would require stopping the deployment, and ArgoCD's selfHeal reverts a manual scale to zero.

docs.title: Provisioning an account instead
docs.text:
POST /v1/auth/web/start creates a user through the application's own code path when signup is open. Flip SYNC_ALLOW_SIGNUP to "true" in apps/td-sync/k8s.td-sync.yaml, push, wait for the rollout, then:

curl -sS -X POST https://td.internal.neese-web.de/v1/auth/web/start \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"<address>","redirect_uri":"https://td.internal.neese-web.de/","state":"bootstrap"}'

The response is always {"status":"email_sent_if_allowed",...} — it reveals nothing either way, so verify the result directly:

kubectl exec -n td-sync deploy/td-sync -- \
  sqlite3 /data/server.db "SELECT id, email, is_admin FROM users;"

Then set SYNC_ALLOW_SIGNUP back to "false" and push. The first user created becomes an admin automatically.

Do not hand-write the row with sqlite3: CreateUser generates a prefixed id, decides admin status from the current user count, and writes timestamps in the driver's format.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
td-sync has no SMTP provider configured, so the magic link that td auth login triggers is retrieved from the server's dev inspection endpoint rather than an inbox.

export TD_ENABLE_FEATURE=sync_cli   # sync commands are behind this feature flag
td config set sync.url https://td.internal.neese-web.de
td auth login

td auth login sends the email and waits. Fetch the link it generated:

curl -s https://td.internal.neese-web.de/internal/dev/last-email | jq -r .text

Open the printed /auth/device/approve?token=... URL in a browser to approve the login. Links expire after 15 minutes. The in-memory email provider holds only the single most recent email and loses it on pod restart, so re-run td auth login if too much time passes between the two steps.

docs.title: Security note
docs.text: GET /internal/dev/last-email is unauthenticated and returns the full body of the most recently sent login email — including the magic link token in plaintext — to anyone who can reach the ingress. This is enabled deliberately (SYNC_EMAIL_PROVIDER=memory + SYNC_DEV_EMAIL_INSPECT=true) as a trade-off for a single-user deployment with no SMTP relay available. Anyone who can reach https://td.internal.neese-web.de during the ~15 minute window after a login attempt can complete that login.

docs.title: Other admin subcommands
docs.text:
td-sync admin also provides:

  • grant - grant a user access to a project
  • revoke - revoke a user's access to a project
  • create-key - create an API key
  • revoke-key - revoke an API key

Run any of them the same way, via kubectl exec -n td-sync deploy/td-sync --.

docs.title: Test environment
docs.text: The test environment is based upon virtual machines and created with Vagrant and libvirt. You need a quiet powerful machine to run the full test environment. It can create up to three systems with the following configuration:

docs.title: Virtual Machine Specifications
docs.text:
• k3svm1: The server node of the k3s cluster
    • 4096MB RAM
    • 4 CPU threads
    • Role: k3s server (control plane)
  • k3svm2: The first worker node of the k3s cluster
    • 2048MB RAM
    • 2 CPU threads
    • Role: k3s server (control plane)
  • k3svm3: The second worker node of the k3s cluster
    • 2048MB RAM
    • 2 CPU threads
    • Role: k3s agent (worker)

Total resources required: 8192MB RAM and 8 CPU threads when running all three VMs.

docs.title: Architecture Decision
docs.text: I decided to base the test environment on virtual machines because I also test different network plugins. This is much easier to do with virtual machines than with containers. Another requirement is ansible, which I use to initially install k3s. This also needs to be tested. During deployment Vagrant uses the same ansible playbook to provision the system(s) as the one used for the production environment. Just the vars are a bit different and can be adjusted in the ansible/inventory/vagrant/group_vars/all/main.yaml file.

docs.title: File Organization
docs.text:
In the subfolder ./shared/${HOSTNAME}/ are files for the configuration of the k3s cluster, like the kubeconfig.

The folder ./shared gets also mounted to the virtual machines. This is the place where you can put files you want to share with the virtual machines. Though this requires memory_backing_dir = "/dev/shm" in /etc/libvirt/qemu.conf.

libvirt Configuration Required

The shared folder mounting requires the following configuration in /etc/libvirt/qemu.conf: 

memory_backing_dir = "/dev/shm"
After changing this setting, restart libvirtd: 
sudo systemctl restart libvirtd

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before setting up the test environment, ensure you have:

  • Virtualization support: CPU with VT-x/AMD-V enabled in BIOS
  • libvirt: KVM/QEMU virtualization platform installed
  • Vagrant: Version 2.3.0 or higher
  • Sufficient resources: At least 8GB free RAM and 8 CPU threads for full cluster
  • Disk space: Minimum 20GB free for VM images and data

docs.title: Setting up vagrant
docs.text:
At first install vagrant for your system. This wont be covered here. Please refer to the vagrant documentation.

Add the libvirt plugin:

vagrant plugin install vagrant-libvirt

Using Docker Container (Recommended)

If you have, like me, dependency problems with the libvirt plugin, you can use the vagrant-libvirt docker container. I recommend you to use my extended vagrant-libvirt-ansible container with added ansible. Ansible is required for provisioning and by default not installed in the standard vagrant-libvirt container.

To use the container: 

docker run -it --rm \
  -v /var/run/libvirt/:/var/run/libvirt/ \
  -v ~/.vagrant.d:/root/.vagrant.d \
  -v $(pwd):$(pwd) \
  -w $(pwd) \
  --network host \
  ghcr.io/madic-creates/vagrant-libvirt-ansible:latest \
  vagrant up

docs.title: Full Cluster Deployment
docs.text:
Start the complete test environment with all three nodes:

vagrant up

This will:

  1. Create three VMs (k3svm1, k3svm2, k3svm3)
  2. Run the Ansible playbook ansible/playbooks/install.yaml
  3. Install k3s on the server node
  4. Join worker nodes to the cluster
  5. Copy kubeconfig to shared/k3svm1/k3s.yaml

Provisioning Time

The initial provisioning can take 10-15 minutes depending on your system resources and internet connection. After the Vagrant provisioning completes, allow an additional 2-3 minutes for k3s to fully initialize.

docs.title: Single Node Deployment
docs.text:
Start only the server node (which is enough for many tests):

vagrant up k3svm1

This creates a single-node cluster that is sufficient for testing:

  • Application deployments
  • ArgoCD functionality
  • Kustomize configurations
  • Secret management with SOPS
  • Basic networking

docs.title: Accessing the Cluster
docs.text:
After the installation is finished, it can still take some time till the k3s service is up and running.

The ansible ansible/playbooks/install.yaml playbook, which vagrant automatically runs, will copy the kubeconfig from the server node to shared/k3svm1/k3s.yaml. You can use this file to access the test k3s cluster.

Set the KUBECONFIG environment variable:

export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/shared/k3svm1/k3s.yaml"

Verify cluster access:

kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A

docs.title: Adding additional Nodes
docs.text:
Start the worker nodes separately if needed. Ansible will automatically join the worker nodes to the k3s cluster.

vagrant up k3svm2
vagrant up k3svm3

When to Use Worker Nodes

Worker nodes are useful for testing:

  • Multi-node scheduling
  • Pod anti-affinity rules
  • Node selectors and taints
  • Storage replication (Longhorn)
  • High availability scenarios

docs.title: SSH Access
docs.text:
Once your virtual machine is up and running, you can log in to it:

vagrant ssh k3svm1

Useful commands inside the VM:

# Check k3s service status
sudo systemctl status k3s

# View k3s logs on control-plane
sudo journalctl -u k3s -f

# View k3s logs on worker
sudo journalctl -u k3s-agent -f

# Check node resources
kubectl top nodes

docs.title: Destroying the Environment
docs.text:
Destroy the test environment and reclaim resources:

vagrant destroy -f

To destroy a specific VM:

vagrant destroy k3svm2 -f

docs.title: Deploying Applications
docs.text:
Once the cluster is running, you can test application deployments:

# Build kustomization locally
kubectl kustomize apps/myapp --enable-helm

# Apply directly (for testing without ArgoCD)
kubectl kustomize apps/myapp --enable-helm | kubectl apply -f -

# Check deployment status
kubectl get pods -n myapp-namespace
kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n myapp-namespace

docs.title: Testing ArgoCD
docs.text:
Deploy ArgoCD to the test cluster:

# Deploy ArgoCD
kubectl kustomize apps/argo-cd --enable-helm | kubectl apply -f -

# Wait for ArgoCD to be ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=available --timeout=300s deployment/argocd-server -n argocd

# Get admin password
kubectl get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -n argocd -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d

Port-forward to access ArgoCD UI:

kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443

docs.title: Testing Network Policies
docs.text:
When testing Cilium network policies, use Hubble:

# Install Cilium CLI in the VM
vagrant ssh k3svm1
curl -L --remote-name-all https://github.com/cilium/cilium-cli/releases/latest/download/cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz
sudo tar xzvfC cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz /usr/local/bin
rm cilium-linux-amd64.tar.gz

# Enable Hubble port-forward
cilium hubble port-forward &

# Observe traffic from your namespace
hubble observe --namespace myapp --last 100

docs.title: Vagrant Snapshots
docs.text:
Create snapshots for quick rollback:

# Take a snapshot
vagrant snapshot save k3svm1 clean-state

# List snapshots
vagrant snapshot list

# Restore snapshot
vagrant snapshot restore k3svm1 clean-state

# Delete snapshot
vagrant snapshot delete k3svm1 clean-state

docs.title: Vagrant Issues
docs.text:
Sometimes vagrant has conflicts with OS packages resulting in messages like this:

conflicting dependencies date (= 3.2.2) and date (= 3.3.4)

Set the following environment variable to ignore gem versions or directly use my vagrant-libvirt-ansible container:

export VAGRANT_DISABLE_STRICT_DEPENDENCY_ENFORCEMENT=1

docs.title: VM Won't Start
docs.text:
Check libvirt status:

sudo systemctl status libvirtd
sudo virsh list --all

View libvirt logs:

sudo journalctl -u libvirtd -f

docs.title: k3s Service Not Starting
docs.text:
SSH into the VM and check k3s status:

vagrant ssh k3svm1
sudo systemctl status k3s
sudo journalctl -u k3s --no-pager -n 50

docs.title: Kubeconfig Not Working
docs.text:
Ensure the kubeconfig file exists:

ls -la shared/k3svm1/k3s.yaml

If missing, manually copy from VM:

vagrant ssh k3svm1 -c "sudo cat /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml" | sed "s/127.0.0.1/$(vagrant ssh-config k3svm1 | grep HostName | awk '{print $2}')/g" > shared/k3svm1/k3s.yaml

docs.title: Cleaning Up
docs.text:
If VMs are in an inconsistent state:

# Stop all VMs
vagrant halt

# Destroy all VMs
vagrant destroy -f

# Clean libvirt domains
sudo virsh list --all
sudo virsh undefine k3svm1
sudo virsh undefine k3svm2
sudo virsh undefine k3svm3

# Remove storage
sudo virsh vol-list default
sudo virsh vol-delete k3svm1.img default

docs.title: Reducing Resource Usage
docs.text:
For limited hardware, modify the Vagrantfile to reduce resources:

# Example modifications
config.vm.define "k3svm1" do |node|
  node.vm.provider :libvirt do |libvirt|
    libvirt.memory = 2048  # Reduced from 4096
    libvirt.cpus = 2       # Reduced from 4
  end
end

docs.title: Update management
docs.text:
The cluster uses two components to manage updates:

  • Renovate
  • System Upgrade Controller

docs.title: Renovate
docs.text:
Renovate is configured as a scheduled github workflow. Additionally, the action can be run manually with optional increased debug log or in dry-run mode. As RENOVATE_TOKEN a github personal access token is used.

More information about the required token permissions can be found in the official docs: https://docs.renovatebot.com/modules/platform/github/. I keep it here because I had a hard time finding thoses information 🙈

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Multiple configurations in the renovate.json support renovate in finding updates.

Kubernetes Manifests

Renovate identifies Kubernetes manifests depending on the file name. The current regex is apps\/.+\/k8s\\..*\\.yaml$. Basically beneath the apps folder it matches every yaml file that begins with k8s.

Danger

Renovate must not change Kubernetes manifests which contain sops encrypted entries because that would break the file signature. Encrypted Kubernetes manifests aren't allowed to begin with k8s!

Auto Updates

Renovate will auto-update every entry after 5 days of release. If not explicitly excluded, every minor and patch release gets automatically updated / merged. Major releases need to be approved via Pull Request.

Longhorn is an exception. It will never automerge and will only create Pull Requests for releases that are available for 14 days, even for patch releases. Because Longhorn is the storage provider for the cluster, I want it to be a tested release.

Image Tags

Beside updating image tags in kubernetes manifests, renovate updates image tags in kustomization.yaml files when it finds the keyword image or the following structure:

repository: emby/embyserver
tag: 4.9.0.30

Repository is required for renovate to know, in which repository to search for new versions to update the tag.

Image Tags in Helm Values (values.public.yaml)

Renovate cannot read SOPS-encrypted files (values.enc.yaml). To allow Renovate to update image tags in Helm values, non-sensitive values are extracted into a plaintext values.public.yaml file. See Secret Management - Pattern 2 for details on the split pattern.

A custom manager in renovate.json5 scans values.public.yaml files for the same repository + tag structure:

values.public.yaml
image:
    repository: ghcr.io/pi-hole/pihole
    tag: 2025.11.0

pre-commit hooks

Renovate is able to update pre-commit hooks. But it's still in beta and can lead to problems. Because of this automerge for pre-commit is disabled and every update requires approval through a pull request.

docs.title: Dependency Dashboard
docs.text:
Renovate keeps its state in the "Dependency Dashboard" issue. The dashboard can lag behind main by several hours, for example still listing an old chart version under "Detected Dependencies" or showing a PR as open after it has been merged. That is how Renovate works, not a sign that the workflow is broken.

Renovate only rewrites the dashboard when a repository run finishes without an automerge. When a branch automerges, Renovate restarts the run once on the new main. If the restarted run automerges again, it stops without touching the dashboard ("Automerged but already retried once", see lib/workers/repository/index.ts in Renovate 44). With many minor/patch automerges queued, several scheduled runs in a row can end like this, and the dashboard stays at the last run that had nothing left to automerge.

To check whether the dashboard is just behind:

  • Compare the issue's last update time with the latest workflow runs. Each run logs "result": "automerged" or "result": "done" under "Repository finished". Only done runs update the dashboard.
  • The dashboard catches up on its own once a run has nothing left to automerge. To force that sooner, trigger the workflow manually (repeat if that run also automerges).

docs.title: System Upgrade Controller
docs.text:
The System Upgrade Controller is a Kubernetes controller that manages the upgrade of a Kubernetes cluster. There are only plans configured to automatically upgrade the cluster to the latest k3s version.

The update plans are a separate ArgoCD app because they require CRDs from the system-upgrade-controller. Without those CRDs ArgoCD would not be able to apply the plans and the deployment would fail if they are included in the system-upgrade-controller app.

docs.title: Backup migration: Wasabi-only → local-first with Wasabi mirror
docs.text:
This runbook covers the one-time migration from the Wasabi-only backup architecture to the local-first architecture introduced by the backup-rest-server app. Run it from a workstation with kubectl access and an ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt containing the cluster age key.

The cluster-side YAML changes already exist in git. Do not push them to ArgoCD until the migration is complete — the new backup secrets point to a rest-server that has no repository yet, and any backup CronJob that fires before the initial copy will fail.

docs.title: 0. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• restic ≥ 0.16 on the workstation
  • kubectl configured for the production cluster
  • sops and the cluster age key (~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt)
  • Workstation can resolve and reach Wasabi
  • Optional: a coffee — the initial copy is the slow step

docs.title: 1. Provision the ZFS dataset on node04
docs.text:
ssh into node04 and create a dedicated dataset for the local repo:

sudo zfs create vol_raidz1/restic-local
sudo zfs set compression=zstd vol_raidz1/restic-local
sudo zfs set atime=off vol_raidz1/restic-local
sudo zfs set quota=200G vol_raidz1/restic-local      # adjust to taste
sudo chown 65534:65534 /vol_raidz1/restic-local
sudo chmod 700 /vol_raidz1/restic-local

The dataset must be owned by UID 65534 — the same user the rest-server pod and all backup-related CronJobs run as. The chmod 700 is defensive; the contents are restic-encrypted anyway.

docs.title: 2. Deploy rest-server only (without flipping the workloads)
docs.text:
The apps/backup-rest-server/ ArgoCD Application should sync first. The other YAML changes (backup secrets, NetworkPolicies) are already committed but ArgoCD has not seen them yet.

If ArgoCD auto-sync is enabled and the changes are already pushed, pause it for the affected applications before pushing:

kubectl annotate application -n argocd 15-backup-rest-server \
  argocd.argoproj.io/sync-policy=Manual --overwrite

for app in 08-mariadb 16-monitoring 30-emby 31-nextpvr \
           40-paperless-ngx 65-nzbget 15-backup-script; do
  kubectl annotate application -n argocd "$app" \
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-policy=Manual --overwrite
done

Push the branch / let CI propagate it. Then sync only 15-backup-rest-server:

argocd app sync 15-backup-rest-server
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available -n backup deploy/rest-server --timeout=5m
kubectl logs -n backup -l app.kubernetes.io/name=rest-server --tail=10

Immediately after the sync, suspend the Wasabi mirror CronJob until the migration is complete. Both targets share the Wasabi bucket during the migration window — workload backups still push to Wasabi (until step 6), the workstation restic copy reads from Wasabi, and the mirror would write local → Wasabi. Most restic files are content-addressed and cannot collide, but lock files and the config blob are not, and running the mirror against a bucket that retention is also pruning risks resurrecting deleted index files. Cleaner to keep the mirror off:

kubectl patch cronjob -n backup backup-mirror-wasabi \
  -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'

Confirm rest-server is healthy. Read the rest-server password from the encrypted Secret on disk and pipe it through curl:

REST_PW=$(sops --config .sops.yaml -d \
  apps/backup-rest-server/secrets.enc.yaml \
  | yq -r '.stringData.htpasswd' | awk -F: '{print $2}')
# (just for the manual smoke test below — the real password lives in
# every backup-secrets.enc.yaml under RESTIC_REPOSITORY)

kubectl run -n backup --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=curlimages/curl curltest -- \
  sh -c 'echo "Use a per-target backup-secrets.enc.yaml or ksops-decoded value"'
# Expected: empty 200 response (or "Restic REST Server" body) when
# you supply -u backup:<password>

docs.title: 3. Initialize the empty local repo
docs.text:
From the workstation, port-forward the rest-server and restic init. Pull the credentials from the existing encrypted Secrets — never hard-code them in this document:

kubectl port-forward -n backup svc/rest-server 8000:8000 &
PF_PID=$!

# Decrypt one of the backup target secrets and reuse its values.
# Any backup-secrets.enc.yaml works — they all share the same
# repository password and rest-server URL.
eval "$(sops --config .sops.yaml -d apps/monitoring/backup-grafana-secrets.enc.yaml \
  | yq -r '.stringData | to_entries[] | "export \(.key)='\(.value)'"' \
  | grep -E '^export RESTIC_(REPOSITORY|PASSWORD)=')"

# Override the in-cluster service URL with the local port-forward.
export RESTIC_REPOSITORY="${RESTIC_REPOSITORY/rest-server.backup.svc.cluster.local/127.0.0.1}"

restic init
restic snapshots          # should print "no snapshots found"

kill $PF_PID

docs.title: 4. Copy snapshots from Wasabi
docs.text:
Still from the workstation, set up the source (Wasabi) and target (local rest-server) and run restic copy. This is the slow part — expect ~2–8 hours for a ~180 GB Wasabi repo, depending on workstation download speed.

kubectl port-forward -n backup svc/rest-server 8000:8000 &
PF_PID=$!

# Pull both Wasabi and rest-server credentials from encrypted secrets.
eval "$(sops --config .sops.yaml -d apps/backup-rest-server/mirror-secrets.enc.yaml \
  | yq -r '.stringData | to_entries[] | "export \(.key)='\(.value)'"' \
  | grep -E '^export AWS_(ACCESS_KEY_ID|SECRET_ACCESS_KEY)=')"

# Source: Wasabi
export RESTIC_FROM_REPOSITORY='s3:s3.eu-central-2.wasabisys.com/k3s-at-home-01/restic-backup'
# Both repos share the same encryption password — already exported via
# RESTIC_PASSWORD in step 3. RESTIC_FROM_PASSWORD defaults to it.

# Target: local rest-server (already in $RESTIC_REPOSITORY from step 3)

restic copy --from-repo "$RESTIC_FROM_REPOSITORY"
# Run with --verbose for progress; restic groups output by snapshot.

kill $PF_PID

For long initial copies, prefer the in-cluster Job approach (no port-forward fragility): a one-shot Job in the backup namespace that injects the credentials from existing Secrets. The Job pattern is documented separately and reuses the backup-mirror-wasabi-creds Secret for Wasabi and any of the per-target backup secrets for rest-server.

Both repos use the same encryption password, so restic copy is a straight blob-copy without re-encryption.

If the copy is interrupted, just restart it — restic copy is idempotent and skips snapshots that already exist on the destination.

docs.title: 5. Verify the local repo
docs.text:
kubectl port-forward -n backup svc/rest-server 8000:8000 &
PF_PID=$!

restic snapshots                      # should mirror Wasabi
restic stats --mode raw-data          # repo size on disk
restic check --read-data-subset 5%    # spot-check pack files

kill $PF_PID

The snapshots count should match what's in Wasabi (modulo a handful that may have been pushed during the copy).

docs.title: 6. Flip the workloads
docs.text:
Re-enable auto-sync on the Applications you paused:

for app in 15-backup-rest-server 08-mariadb 16-monitoring 30-emby \
           31-nextpvr 40-paperless-ngx 65-nzbget 15-backup-script; do
  kubectl annotate application -n argocd "$app" \
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-policy- --overwrite
done

# Or sync them all at once:
for app in 08-mariadb 16-monitoring 30-emby 31-nextpvr \
           40-paperless-ngx 65-nzbget 15-backup-script; do
  argocd app sync "$app"
done

ArgoCD updates the backup secrets (now pointing at rest-server) and the NetworkPolicies (egress to rest-server, ntfy only on the public internet). The next backup hour each CronJob fires writes its snapshot into the local rest-server.

docs.title: 7. Smoke-test each backup target
docs.text:
Trigger one manual run per target and confirm it lands in the local repo:

for ns_cron in databases/backup-mariadb monitoring/backup-grafana \
               media/backup-emby media/backup-nextpvr \
               downloader/backup-downloader paper/backup-paperless; do
  ns="${ns_cron%/*}"; cron="${ns_cron#*/}"
  kubectl create job -n "$ns" --from="cronjob/$cron" "$cron-smoke"
done

# Watch the logs as they start to land:
kubectl logs -n monitoring -l job-name=backup-grafana-smoke -f

Verify that snapshots accumulate locally:

kubectl port-forward -n backup svc/rest-server 8000:8000 &
restic snapshots --tag mariadb --last 1
restic snapshots --tag grafana --last 1
restic snapshots --tag emby --last 1
restic snapshots --tag nextpvr --last 1
restic snapshots --tag downloader --last 1
restic snapshots --tag paperless --last 1

docs.title: 8. Re-enable and smoke-test the Wasabi mirror
docs.text:
Now that the workloads write to local and no other process is touching the Wasabi bucket, it's safe to flip the mirror back on:

kubectl patch cronjob -n backup backup-mirror-wasabi \
  -p '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}'

Trigger the daily mirror once to confirm the pipeline works end-to-end:

kubectl create job -n backup \
  --from=cronjob/backup-mirror-wasabi backup-mirror-smoke
kubectl logs -n backup -l job-name=backup-mirror-smoke -f

The first run should be a near-no-op — Wasabi already has every blob the local repo just received via step 4. From then on the daily 05:00 slot keeps Wasabi in sync.

docs.title: 9. Clean up the legacy Wasabi-direct artifacts
docs.text:
After the first successful daily mirror (and optionally a second day of normal hourly backups going through), the system is steady-state.

Optional cleanup commits (kept out of the migration commit so they land separately):

  • Remove apps/backup-script/rclone-config.enc.yaml and its entry in apps/backup-script/kustomize-secret-generator.yaml — the retention CronJob no longer uses rclone.
  • Tighten any per-app NetworkPolicies that still allow world:443/80 but only need :443 for ntfy (already done in this migration — double-check via kubectl describe ciliumnetworkpolicy).

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If something goes wrong before step 6 (the workload flip), nothing else is affected — Wasabi is still authoritative. Simply scale the rest-server Deployment to 0 and revert the un-pushed git changes.

If something goes wrong after step 6:

  1. Revert the per-target backup secrets back to the Wasabi RESTIC_REPOSITORY URL and re-add AWS_* (the values are still in this runbook above).
  2. Re-apply or argocd app sync each affected Application.
  3. Backups resume going to Wasabi directly.

The local rest-server stays in place — it just receives no new writes. You can leave it running, or scale to 0 and remove the app.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Component URL / location rest-server Service rest-server.backup.svc.cluster.local:8000 Local repo on disk /vol_raidz1/restic-local (node04, owner 65534:65534) Wasabi repo s3:s3.eu-central-2.wasabisys.com/k3s-at-home-01/restic-backup Mirror schedule Daily 05:00 (apps/backup-rest-server/k8s.backup-mirror-wasabi.yaml) Backup user (rest-server) backup Repository password shared, same as before — encrypted in every backup-secrets.enc.yaml

docs.title: Replacing flannel with cilium - live
docs.text: In the beginning the cluster used flannel as cni. I wanted to use cilium so I tested a live migration from flannel to cilium. In short: Only do this if you realy know what you are doing. This is a complex task and requires linux and kubernetes networking knowledge. The following guide is just a starting point. There were many small problems afterwards.

docs.title: Creating test environment
docs.text:
In repository root

vagrant up
# Wait vor all hosts becoming ready
cd apps/overlays/
export KUBECONFIG="$(realpath ../../shared/k3svm1/k3s.yaml)"
kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins --enable-exec ./kubevip-cloud-controller | kubectl apply -f -
kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins --enable-exec ./kubevip-ha | kubectl apply -f -
kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins --enable-exec ./traefik | kubectl apply -f -
kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins --enable-exec ./debug-container | kubectl apply -f -
kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins --enable-exec ./whoami | kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: Migration phase
docs.text:
On all server nodes:

systemctl stop k3s.service

On all agent nodes:

systemctl stop k3s-agent.service

On server nodes add the following parameters in /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml:

nano /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml
flannel-backend: none
disable-kube-proxy: true

On all k3s servers / agents:

ip link delete flannel.1
ip link delete flannel-wg

On all server nodes:

systemctl start k3s.service

On all k3s agents:

systemctl start k3s-agent.service

On localhost or wherever cilium cli is installed:

docs.title: Installing cilium
docs.text:
Delete the following deployments in this order:

  • kubevip-cloud-controller
# The CIDR List must match the cidr range from the previous cni!
# <deployment>
helm repo add cilium https://helm.cilium.io/
helm install cilium cilium/cilium --version 1.17.6 \
   --namespace kube-system \
   -f apps/argo-cd-apps-helm/values.cilium.yaml
cilium status --wait
cilium connectivity test
# Cleanup cilium connectivity test
kubectl delete ns cilium-test-1
# Restart unmanaged pods
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o custom-columns=NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,HOSTNETWORK:.spec.hostNetwork --no-headers=true | grep '<none>' | awk '{print "-n "$1" "$2}' | xargs -L 1 -r kubectl delete pod

Reboot all nodes to re-create all host firewall rules and restart pods!

Don't do this:

kubectl delete pods --all --all-namespaces

docs.title: Longhorn Maintenance Window
docs.text: This guide describes a repeatable procedure to stop workloads in a controlled way for Longhorn upgrades and then restore normal operations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• kubectl with access to the cluster
  • yq to read the maintenance plan
  • Up-to-date checkout of this repository (git pull) so that scripts/scale-maintenance-plan.yaml and scripts/scale-maintenance.sh are available

Note: The affected Argo CD applications ignore replica drift thanks to the spec.ignoreDifferences entries. During the maintenance window they will report as "Degraded" but will not attempt to roll replicas back automatically.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Check status 

    scripts/scale-maintenance.sh status
    Shows the currently configured replicas and any stored original value for each workload.

  2. Stop workloads 

    scripts/scale-maintenance.sh down
    - Stores the current replica count as the annotation maintenance.k3s-git-ops/original-replicas. - Scales the Deployments, StatefulSets, and operator-managed CRs (Prometheus / Alertmanager) listed in scripts/scale-maintenance-plan.yaml down to 0. - The command is idempotent and can be dry-run with --dry-run.

  3. Perform the Longhorn upgrade - Upgrade Longhorn (UI or Argo CD). - Afterwards verify that the storage cluster is healthy.

  4. Restore workloads 

    scripts/scale-maintenance.sh up
    - Reads the stored values and restores the replicas. - Removes the maintenance annotation afterwards.

  5. Post checks 

    scripts/scale-maintenance.sh status
    - Verifies that no maintenance annotations remain (empty STORED column). - Trigger a "Refresh" in Argo CD for affected apps to update their health status.

docs.title: Adjustments
docs.text:
• Add additional workloads to scripts/scale-maintenance-plan.yaml (id, namespace, kind, name).
  • Alternate plans (for other clusters, for example) can be provided via PLAN_FILE=/path/to/plan.yaml or the --plan-file flag.
  • Use --dry-run for a rehearsal without actually touching replicas; the commands will be logged only.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Annotation missing on restore: Confirm that the scale-down completed successfully; otherwise set the desired replica count manually (for Prometheus / Alertmanager CRs: kubectl patch ... --type merge -p '{"spec":{"replicas":<n>}}') and re-run the script.
  • Resource not found: Check namespace and name in the plan. Helm releases with prefixes must match exactly.
  • Argo CD immediately restores replicas: Confirm that the application includes the ignoreDifferences entry and that it has been refreshed after the maintenance window.

docs.title: Power Consumption Audit
docs.text: Findings of a power audit of the four cluster nodes (October 2026, td-08070d). No change to the cluster came out of it directly. The measurable reductions are tracked as separate td issues, listed at the end.

docs.title: Measurement setup
docs.text:
• There is one meter for the whole cluster: the Shelly plug named Server. It measures a power strip with all four nodes on it, not node04 alone.
  • node01-03 have no meter of their own, so a saving on the NUCs cannot be measured today. The NUC rail needs its own plug first.
  • The Shelly readings are scraped by Prometheus (see Monitoring).

docs.title: Baseline
docs.text:
4 hours at 30 s resolution (481 samples):

Statistic Watts median 201.1 p05 191.7 p95 213.4 min / max 187.9 / 238.3 standard deviation 7.4

About 75 % of the draw is a base load that does not depend on CPU load. The 5-95 % band is only 22 W wide.

A regression of the Shelly power against the CPU load of all four nodes has R² = 0.021, with some coefficients negative. That is no signal at all. The total cannot be split per node from correlation alone. It needs a controlled experiment, see below.

docs.title: Per-node load experiment
docs.text:
td-866186 put one node at a time under full CPU load and read the change on the Server plug. Each node got 6 minutes of load: one niced shell busy loop per hardware thread, stopped by timeout. Every load window had a 6-minute idle window before and after it. The first 60 s of each window were dropped, which leaves 10 samples per window at the 30 s scrape interval.

Window Mean (W) Min (W) Max (W) idle 191.7 185.3 199.2 load node01 240.6 229.8 277.0 idle 201.7 186.8 223.2 load node02 240.6 232.1 253.1 idle 193.6 185.0 209.3 load node03 229.5 225.7 234.7 idle 196.5 187.8 209.5 load node04 232.8 226.8 241.2 idle 202.0 191.2 232.7

The delta is the load window minus the mean of the idle windows on either side:

Node CPU Delta under full load node01 i5-10210U, 4C/8T +44 W node02 i5-10210U, 4C/8T +43 W node03 i5-10210U, 4C/8T +34 W node04 Ryzen 5 3600, 6C/12T +34 W

What this means:

  • The NUC BIOS raises the RAPL limits far above the 15 W TDP of the i5-10210U: PL1 (long term) is 30 W, PL2 (short term) is 64 W. A loaded NUC therefore draws 35-45 W more at the wall. That is the PL1 package limit plus voltage regulator and power supply losses.
  • At idle, the three NUCs together are only a small part of the ~195 W total. Under load, each of them can add as much as node04.
  • node04 adds the least relative to its size. A scalar shell loop does not reach the Ryzen package power limit; AVX-heavy work would draw more.
  • The idle windows vary by 10 W (191.7-202.0 W). Treat the deltas as ±5 W.
  • This measures how much each node adds under load, not how the idle draw is split. Splitting the idle draw needs one node at a time powered off, or a separate plug on the NUC rail (td-8da11b).

docs.title: node04 (AMD, storage and GPU node)
docs.text:
• CPU: 94 % idle, amd-pstate-epp, governor powersave, EPP balance_performance. Deepest C-state (C2/CC6) residency 88 %.
  • Estimated share of the total: 155-170 W. This is an estimate, not a measurement.
  • Static consumers that governor tuning cannot reduce, together about 45-50 W:
    • LSI SAS2008 HBA (mpt3sas, link downgraded to PCIe 5 GT/s x4): typically 9-14 W.
    • RTX 3060 Ti: 13.9 W in P8 (measured with nvidia-smi).
    • 4x WD 10 TB disks: about 20-24 W.
  • The disks are 1.3 % busy each, but see 4-6 write operations per second all the time, because the k3s and Longhorn datasets live in the same ZFS pool. Spinning the disks down is not possible without moving that data.
  • SATA link power management is med_power_with_dipm, PCIe ASPM policy is default. There is no modprobe.d or udev tuning.

docs.title: GPU idle power
docs.text:
Scaling all llama-cpp Deployments to 0 replicas did not lower the GPU draw: it stayed at 13.83 W in P8 with 1 MiB VRAM in use and no process on the card. The nvidia driver stays loaded and PCIe runtime PM for the card (07:00.0) is on, so the card never drops below P8.

Scaling llama-cpp down therefore saves no power. The llama-cpp Deployments are scaled by hand on demand, so 0 live replicas is a normal state. ArgoCD ignores replicas for these Deployments (see apps/argo-cd-apps/65-llama-cpp.yaml).

The driver's runtime D3 power management cannot help on this board (td-709827). Powering the card off at idle needs D3cold, which requires ACPI _PR3 power resources on the PCIe root port. The root port of the card (00:03.1, \_SB_.PCI0.GPP8) has none. The driver (nvidia-open-lts 595.71.05) already runs with DynamicPowerManagement=3 (auto) and reports Runtime D3 status: Disabled by default in /proc/driver/nvidia/gpus/0000:07:00.0/power. Forcing NVreg_DynamicPowerManagement=0x02 would not change that.

The card stays installed, so about 14 W in P8 is the idle floor of the GPU on node04.

docs.title: node01-03 (Intel NUC10i5FNH, i5-10210U)
docs.text:
• intel_pstate, governor powersave, EPP balance_performance, turbo enabled.
  • intel_idle with C1-C10 available. SATA link power management min_power_with_partial, PCIe ASPM policy default.
  • No WLAN or Bluetooth module. All display connectors are disconnected.
  • CPU busy: node01 12.7 %, node02 11.7 %, node03 8.5 %.
  • Interrupts: 16-27k/s, context switches 27-50k/s, 32-36 veth interfaces per node.
  • The package never goes below PC3. pmc_core shows 0 residency in package C6 to C10 and 0 for slp_s0 on node01 and node02. The cores reach CC10, but the package does not. See below.

docs.title: Why the NUC package stays at PC3
docs.text:
td-74ae82 tested the usual blockers one at a time on node01 and node02, measuring the pmc_core package residency over 20-30 s windows. None of them moved PC6 off 0:

Suspect Test Result BIOS package C-state limit MSR_PKG_CST_CONFIG_CONTROL (0xE2) = 0x1e008008 Limit nibble 8 = PC10 allowed. Not a limit. GL9755 SD card reader (02:00.0, link with ASPM disabled, stuck in D0) Removed the device through sysfs, root port went to D3hot No change Display on node02 (a monitor on DP-1 kept pipe A lit, DC3 -> DC5 count 0) Unplugged monitor and USB keyboard, DC5 entries started No change I219-V GbE link (e1000e, 1 Gb/s) eno1 down for 20 s No change iGPU render power state rc6_residency_ms 100 % RC6. Not a blocker.

The most likely explanation is the wakeup rate. This is an inference, not a confirmed cause: no test reduced the wakeup rate and showed PC6 appear. node01 takes about 11,300 local timer interrupts per second, roughly 1,400 per thread. That is above the 1,000 Hz kernel tick even with NO_HZ_FULL, so the timers come from userspace (k3s, etcd, Cilium, kubelet, containerd). Each thread idles into CC10 on its own, but all eight threads are almost never idle at the same time for long enough. MSR 0xE2 has C-state auto-demotion enabled, so the hardware demotes those short package idles to PC3.

If that is right, this is the cost of running a Kubernetes control-plane node, not a misconfiguration. PCIe ASPM policy powersupersave and EPP power were not tested (td-831b31). The saving from PC6+ on a 15 W NUC is estimated at 1-2 W per node at best; it has not been measured yet (td-3135c2, needs the NUC plug from td-8da11b). That is not worth cutting cluster services for, so no change was made.

The node02 display finding still matters: a monitor left on a node keeps the display out of its power states.

Left over from the tests: the GL9755 SD reader on node01 and node02 is still removed through sysfs until a pci rescan or reboot (td-c6b050), node03 was not measured because it asks for a sudo password (td-64e4c9), and the monitor and keyboard on node02 are still unplugged (td-9aa0c8).

docs.title: Longhorn backup target poll on node01
docs.text: longhorn backup ls --volume-only s3://... runs about every 300 s and takes 100-200 % CPU (2 cores) on node01. Folding the Shelly series on a 300 s period shows a median of 207.9 W in the bucket where the poll runs, against about 200.4 W in all other nine buckets (48 samples per bucket). The peak is about 7 W, but the duty cycle is about 1/10, so the mean cost is only 0.7-1.5 W. This is worth fixing as a configuration issue, not as a power saving.

docs.title: Follow-up issues

docs.title: llama.cpp on k3s with NVIDIA GPU — Implementation Plan
docs.text:
For agentic workers: REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (- [ ]) syntax for tracking.

Goal: Deploy two new ArgoCD applications to this k3s cluster — nvidia-device-plugin (advertises nvidia.com/gpu as a schedulable resource on node04) and llama-cpp (an OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint at https://llama.internal.neese-web.de running Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct Q4_K_M with 32 k context, agent-tuned).

Architecture: Two GitOps apps, deployed in dependency order via ArgoCD sync waves (24 → 65). Phase 1 must be live and advertising nvidia.com/gpu on node04 before Phase 2 begins. The model file is staged manually on node04 under /zfs/llama-cpp/models/ and verified at pod startup by an init container (file existence + GGUF magic bytes + pinned SHA256). All secrets are SOPS-encrypted; ksops decrypts them at kustomize build time. Auth is a single shared bearer token enforced by llama.cpp's --api-key-file. Ingress is plain networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress annotated for Traefik on the internal entrypoint pair.

Tech Stack: k3s v1.31 · ArgoCD · Kustomize + Helm · ksops + SOPS + age · Cilium NetworkPolicies · Traefik ingress · cert-manager (existing wildcard cert) · NVIDIA k8s-device-plugin (Helm) · llama.cpp server (CUDA build) · Renovate.

Approved spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-09-llama-cpp-design.md. If anything in this plan disagrees with the spec, the spec wins — stop and fix the plan first.

docs.title: Conventions for this plan
docs.text:
• The cluster is the source of truth for whether something works. After every push, watch kubectl get application -n argocd <app> until SYNC=Synced HEALTH=Healthy.
  • "Test" in this plan = (a) kustomize build succeeds without error, (b) scripts/kubeconform-validate.sh passes, (c) pre-commit run --all-files is green. After deploy, also (d) kubectl queries return the expected state and (e) HTTP smoke tests against the endpoint succeed.
  • All commits go on main. Push only after the full pre-commit suite is green.
  • Never kubectl edit / kubectl apply an ArgoCD-managed object. Edit YAML, commit, push, wait for sync.
  • All code comments inside YAML/scripts must be in English (see CLAUDE.md).
  • The encrypted-file workflow is documented in CLAUDE.md ("Editing SOPS files from Claude Code"). Use Workflow B (decrypt to /tmp, edit, re-encrypt) for the multi-line files in this plan.

The spec leaves the Helm chart version unpinned. Pick the current stable from upstream and lock it.

Files: none yet — this task only resolves a value used in Task 1.4.

helm repo update nvdp
helm search repo nvdp/nvidia-device-plugin --versions | head -5

Pick the latest non-prerelease entry. Record it for Task 1.4 — call it <CHART_VERSION> for the rest of this phase.

Write the version to a scratch file the engineer can refer back to:

docs.title: Task 1.3: Network policies
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/nvidia-device-plugin/k8s.np.nvidia-device-plugin-default-deny.yaml - Create: apps/nvidia-device-plugin/k8s.np.nvidia-device-plugin.yaml

The default-deny is the standard pattern used by every namespace in this repo. The allow-policy mirrors apps/intel-gpu/k8s.np.intel-gpu.yaml — the device-plugin DaemonSet pattern is the same for both vendors.

  • Step 1: Default-deny policy

apps/nvidia-device-plugin/k8s.np.nvidia-device-plugin-default-deny.yaml:

---
# Default Deny Network Policy for namespace
# Applies to ALL pods in the namespace and provides the baseline rule
# that all pods inherit.
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: nvidia-device-plugin-default-deny
  namespace: nvidia-device-plugin
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingress:
    - {}
  egress:
    - {}
  • Step 2: Allow policy for the device plugin DaemonSet

apps/nvidia-device-plugin/k8s.np.nvidia-device-plugin.yaml:

---
# NVIDIA Device Plugin Network Policy
# The device plugin DaemonSet runs on nodes with NVIDIA GPUs and registers
# GPU resources with the kubelet. It needs:
# 1. To accept gRPC from the kubelet (host) on the device-plugin socket
# 2. DNS resolution
# 3. Outbound to host (kubelet) and the kube-apiserver
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: nvidia-device-plugin
  namespace: nvidia-device-plugin
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "24"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: nvidia-device-plugin
  ingress:
    # Kubelet -> device plugin (registration + AllocateResponse)
    - fromEntities:
        - host
  egress:
    # DNS via CoreDNS
    - toEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            k8s:io.cilium.k8s.namespace.labels.kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
            k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
            k8s:k8s-app: kube-dns
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "53"
              protocol: UDP
            - port: "53"
              protocol: TCP
    # Device plugin -> kubelet (host) over the device-plugin socket
    - toEntities:
        - host
    # Device plugin -> kube-apiserver for node status
    - toEntities:
        - kube-apiserver

Note on the endpointSelector label. The NVIDIA chart sets the standard app.kubernetes.io/name=nvidia-device-plugin label on the DaemonSet pod template. If Task 1.6 reveals different labels in the rendered manifest, update this selector accordingly before Task 1.7.

  • Step 3: Yamllint sanity check
pre-commit run --files apps/nvidia-device-plugin/k8s.np.*.yaml

Expected: PASS.

docs.title: Task 1.4: Kustomization with Helm chart
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/nvidia-device-plugin/kustomization.yaml

  • Step 1: Write kustomization.yaml

Replace <CHART_VERSION> with the value resolved in Task 1.1.

---
namespace: nvidia-device-plugin

resources:
  - namespace.yaml
  - k8s.np.nvidia-device-plugin-default-deny.yaml
  - k8s.np.nvidia-device-plugin.yaml

helmCharts:
  - name: nvidia-device-plugin
    repo: https://nvidia.github.io/k8s-device-plugin
    version: <CHART_VERSION>
    namespace: nvidia-device-plugin
    releaseName: nvidia-device-plugin
    includeCRDs: true
    valuesInline:
      runtimeClassName: nvidia
      nodeSelector:
        feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-0300_10de.present: "true"

commonAnnotations:
  argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "24"

Why these two values: - runtimeClassName: nvidia — the device-plugin pod itself talks to the NVIDIA driver and needs the NVIDIA runtime; this RuntimeClass already exists cluster-wide. - nodeSelector — the NFD label feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-0300_10de.present is set automatically on any node with an NVIDIA card (vendor 10de). Adding more NVIDIA nodes later requires zero changes here.

docs.title: Task 1.5: ArgoCD Application manifest
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/argo-cd-apps/24-nvidia-device-plugin.yaml

  • Step 1: Create the Application
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: 24-nvidia-device-plugin
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "24"
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: "example.com"
    path: apps/nvidia-device-plugin
    targetRevision: HEAD
  destination:
    server: "https://kubernetes.default.svc"
    namespace: default
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

The repoURL: "example.com" placeholder is intentional — it is rewritten by a kustomize replacement in apps/argo-cd-apps/kustomization.yaml at the parent level using a SOPS-encrypted secret. Do not change it.

docs.title: Task 1.9: Push and observe
docs.text:
Files: none — this is a deploy-and-verify step.

  • Step 1: Push
git push origin main
  • Step 2: Wait for ArgoCD to sync and report Healthy

Poll until both Sync and Health are green:

until kubectl get application -n argocd 24-nvidia-device-plugin \
  -o jsonpath='SYNC={.status.sync.status} HEALTH={.status.health.status}{"\n"}' \
  | tee /dev/stderr | grep -q 'SYNC=Synced HEALTH=Healthy'; do
  sleep 10
done

If it stays OutOfSync for more than ~2 minutes, force a refresh:

kubectl annotate -n argocd application 24-nvidia-device-plugin \
  argocd.argoproj.io/refresh=hard --overwrite
  • Step 3: Verify the GPU is allocatable on node04
kubectl get node node04 -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}{"\n"}'

Expected: 1.

If empty: 1. Check the device-plugin pod is running and on node04: kubectl get pods -n nvidia-device-plugin -o wide 2. Inspect logs for driver/runtime errors: kubectl logs -n nvidia-device-plugin -l app.kubernetes.io/name=nvidia-device-plugin --tail=200

Do not proceed to Phase 2 until nvidia.com/gpu is 1.

docs.title: Phase 2 — llama-cpp
docs.text: Wave 65. Depends on Phase 1 being live and nvidia.com/gpu: 1 allocatable on node04.

docs.title: Task 2.1: Resolve placeholders
docs.text:
The spec lists three placeholders that must be pinned during this phase:

  1. The llama.cpp container image tag (the upstream repo tags every commit b<NNNN>).
  2. The model file SHA256.
  3. The shared API key.

Files: none — this task only resolves values used in later tasks.

  • Step 1: Pick a llama.cpp server-cuda tag

Visit https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pkgs/container/llama.cpp and pick the most recent stable server-cuda-bNNNN tag. Avoid pre-release / nightly tags.

Record it as <LLAMA_IMAGE_TAG> in /tmp/llama-cpp-plan-scratch.txt.

  • Step 2: Generate the API key
openssl rand -hex 32 > /tmp/llama-cpp-api-key
chmod 600 /tmp/llama-cpp-api-key
echo "API_KEY: $(cat /tmp/llama-cpp-api-key)"

Used in Task 2.4. Do not commit this file.

  • Step 3: Decide model file checksum acquisition

The SHA256 cannot be pinned until the file is actually staged on node04 (Task 2.2). The plan sequences it that way: Task 2.2 produces the SHA256, Task 2.6 uses it.

docs.title: Task 2.2: Stage the model file on node04 (manual / out-of-repo)
docs.text:
This is the only step in this plan that mutates host state outside the repo. It must succeed before the deployment can become Ready (the init container will block otherwise).

Files: none in repo. Out-of-repo target: node04:/zfs/llama-cpp/models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf.

  • Step 1: Create the directory and download the model

On the workstation (or by SSHing to node04, depending on how the engineer reaches it):

ssh node04 'sudo mkdir -p /zfs/llama-cpp/models && sudo chown $USER /zfs/llama-cpp/models'

# Download — atomically into a temp name first to avoid partial-file races
ssh node04 'cd /zfs/llama-cpp/models && \
  huggingface-cli download bartowski/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-GGUF \
    Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf \
    --local-dir . --local-dir-use-symlinks False'

# huggingface-cli writes to the final name directly; verify size > 4 GiB
ssh node04 'ls -la /zfs/llama-cpp/models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf'

Expected: file size ~4.4–4.7 GiB (Q4_K_M of a 7B model).

  • Step 2: Compute the SHA256
ssh node04 'sha256sum /zfs/llama-cpp/models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf'

Record the hex value as <MODEL_SHA256> in /tmp/llama-cpp-plan-scratch.txt. Used in Task 2.6.

  • Step 3: Cross-check against HuggingFace

Open https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-GGUF/blob/main/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf in a browser. The "SHA256" shown in the file metadata must match <MODEL_SHA256>. If it does not — stop, the download is corrupt, retry Step 1.

  • Step 4: Lock down permissions
ssh node04 'sudo chmod 644 /zfs/llama-cpp/models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf && \
  sudo chown root:root /zfs/llama-cpp/models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf'

docs.title: Task 2.4: API-key Secret + ksops generator
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/llama-cpp/secrets.enc.yaml (will be encrypted before commit) - Create: apps/llama-cpp/kustomize-secret-generator.yaml

  • Step 1: Write the plaintext Secret to /tmp first

The repo's pre-commit hook blocks unencrypted Secrets in apps/. Write to /tmp initially, encrypt, then move into place.

cat > /tmp/llama-cpp.enc.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp-env
  namespace: llama-cpp
type: Opaque
stringData:
  API_KEY: $(cat /tmp/llama-cpp-api-key)
EOF
  • Step 2: Encrypt in place
sops --config .sops.yaml -e -i /tmp/llama-cpp.enc.yaml

Confirm the file is now encrypted:

grep -q "ENC\[AES256_GCM" /tmp/llama-cpp.enc.yaml && echo OK || echo FAIL

Expected: OK.

  • Step 3: Move into the repo
mv /tmp/llama-cpp.enc.yaml apps/llama-cpp/secrets.enc.yaml
  • Step 4: Verify decryption round-trip
sops --config .sops.yaml -d apps/llama-cpp/secrets.enc.yaml | grep API_KEY

Expected: a single line API_KEY: <the-key> matching /tmp/llama-cpp-api-key.

  • Step 5: ksops generator config

apps/llama-cpp/kustomize-secret-generator.yaml:

---
apiVersion: viaduct.ai/v1
kind: ksops
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp-secret-generator
  annotations:
    config.kubernetes.io/function: |
      exec:
        path: ksops
files:
  - secrets.enc.yaml
  • Step 6: Wipe the plaintext temp file
: > /tmp/llama-cpp-api-key
: > /tmp/llama-cpp.enc.yaml 2>/dev/null || true

The encrypted file is the source of truth from here on. To recover the plaintext key later: sops --config .sops.yaml -d apps/llama-cpp/secrets.enc.yaml.

docs.title: Task 2.5: Network policies
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/llama-cpp/k8s.np.llama-cpp-default-deny.yaml - Create: apps/llama-cpp/k8s.np.llama-cpp.yaml

  • Step 1: Default-deny

apps/llama-cpp/k8s.np.llama-cpp-default-deny.yaml:

---
# Default Deny Network Policy for namespace
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp-default-deny
  namespace: llama-cpp
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}

  • Step 2: Allow Traefik ingress + DNS egress

apps/llama-cpp/k8s.np.llama-cpp.yaml:

---
# llama-cpp Network Policy
# Allows:
# - Ingress from Traefik on port 8080 (the OpenAI API surface)
# - DNS egress (CoreDNS) — required for Service-name resolution at startup
# No other egress: the model is local, no internet access at runtime.
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp
  namespace: llama-cpp
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "65"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: llama-cpp
  ingress:
    # Traefik -> llama-cpp on port 8080
    - fromEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: traefik
            k8s:app.kubernetes.io/name: traefik
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "8080"
              protocol: TCP
  egress:
    # DNS via CoreDNS
    - toEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            k8s:io.cilium.k8s.namespace.labels.kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
            k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
            k8s:k8s-app: kube-dns
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "53"
              protocol: UDP
            - port: "53"
              protocol: TCP

Sanity-check the Traefik label selector after first deploy. Run kubectl get pods -n traefik --show-labels and confirm Traefik pods carry app.kubernetes.io/name=traefik. If the chart uses a different key in this cluster, adjust fromEndpoints.matchLabels accordingly and recommit.

docs.title: Task 2.6: Deployment + Service
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/llama-cpp/k8s.deployment.yaml

This is the largest single file in the plan. It contains the Deployment with init container, the Service, exact args, exact volume mounts, and exact resource requests. Replace the two placeholders below before saving.

Substitutions: - <LLAMA_IMAGE_TAG> — from Task 2.1. - <MODEL_SHA256> — from Task 2.2.

  • Step 1: Write the Deployment + Service

apps/llama-cpp/k8s.deployment.yaml:

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp
  namespace: llama-cpp
  labels:
    app: llama-cpp
spec:
  replicas: 1
  revisionHistoryLimit: 2
  strategy:
    # Single-tenant GPU; rolling would deadlock on nvidia.com/gpu.
    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: llama-cpp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: llama-cpp
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: nvidia
      nodeSelector:
        node-role/workload: zfs
      initContainers:
        # Fail fast with a clear error if the operator forgot to stage the
        # GGUF on node04, or if the file got truncated. Cheaper than a
        # CrashLoop on the main container, which buries the cause in
        # llama.cpp logs.
        - name: verify-model
          image: alpine:3.20
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              set -eu
              MODEL=/models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
              EXPECTED_SHA256=<MODEL_SHA256>
              test -f "$MODEL" || { echo "model file missing: $MODEL"; exit 1; }
              # GGUF magic number is the ASCII string "GGUF" at offset 0
              head -c4 "$MODEL" | grep -q '^GGUF' || {
                echo "not a GGUF file (header mismatch)"; exit 1; }
              echo "$EXPECTED_SHA256  $MODEL" | sha256sum -c -
          volumeMounts:
            - name: models
              mountPath: /models
              readOnly: true
      containers:
        - name: llama-cpp
          image: ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:<LLAMA_IMAGE_TAG>
          args:
            - --model
            - /models/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf
            - --host
            - 0.0.0.0
            - --port
            - "8080"
            - --n-gpu-layers
            - "99"
            - --ctx-size
            - "32768"
            - --cache-type-k
            - q8_0
            - --cache-type-v
            - q8_0
            - --parallel
            - "1"
            - --flash-attn
            - --api-key-file
            - /etc/llama-cpp/api-key
            - --alias
            - qwen2.5-coder-7b
            - --jinja
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 8Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu: 1
            limits:
              cpu: "4"
              memory: 12Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu: 1
          volumeMounts:
            - name: models
              mountPath: /models
              readOnly: true
            - name: api-key
              mountPath: /etc/llama-cpp
              readOnly: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 120  # cold model load can be slow
            periodSeconds: 30
            failureThreshold: 6
      volumes:
        - name: models
          hostPath:
            path: /zfs/llama-cpp/models
            type: Directory
        - name: api-key
          secret:
            secretName: llama-cpp-env
            defaultMode: 0400
            items:
              - key: API_KEY
                path: api-key
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp
  namespace: llama-cpp
spec:
  selector:
    app: llama-cpp
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8080
      targetPort: http
      protocol: TCP
  type: ClusterIP
  • Step 2: Yamllint sanity check
pre-commit run --files apps/llama-cpp/k8s.deployment.yaml

Expected: PASS.

docs.title: Task 2.7: Ingress (encrypted)
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/llama-cpp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml (encrypted before commit)

The hostname is matched by the SOPS encrypted_regex (matches [Hh]osts?), which is why this file is *.enc.yaml. The encryption is purely repo-convention — hostnames are not strictly secret.

  • Step 1: Write the plaintext to /tmp
cat > /tmp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml <<'EOF'
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: llama-cpp
  namespace: llama-cpp
  annotations:
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: web239,websecure239
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.tls: "true"
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.middlewares: traefik-redirect@kubernetescrd
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - llama.internal.neese-web.de
      secretName: wildcard-cloudflare-production-02
  rules:
    - host: llama.internal.neese-web.de
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: llama-cpp
                port:
                  number: 8080
EOF
  • Step 2: Encrypt in place
sops --config .sops.yaml -e -i /tmp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml
grep -q "ENC\[AES256_GCM" /tmp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml && echo OK || echo FAIL

Expected: OK.

  • Step 3: Move into the repo
mv /tmp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml apps/llama-cpp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml
  • Step 4: Round-trip check
sops --config .sops.yaml -d apps/llama-cpp/llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml \
  | grep -E "host:|secretName:" | head -5

Expected: lines for host: llama.internal.neese-web.de and secretName: wildcard-cloudflare-production-02.

docs.title: Task 2.8: Kustomization
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/llama-cpp/kustomization.yaml

  • Step 1: Write kustomization.yaml
---
namespace: llama-cpp

resources:
  - namespace.yaml
  - k8s.deployment.yaml
  - llama-cpp.ingress.enc.yaml
  - k8s.np.llama-cpp-default-deny.yaml
  - k8s.np.llama-cpp.yaml

# ksops decrypts secrets.enc.yaml at build time and produces the Secret as
# if it were a regular resource. secrets.enc.yaml is intentionally NOT in
# `resources:`.
generators:
  - kustomize-secret-generator.yaml

commonAnnotations:
  argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "65"

The encrypted Ingress goes under resources: because Kustomize processes *.enc.yaml resources via the same SOPS+ksops mechanism that the secret generator uses; it is a regular resource at apply time. The Secret is the exception that needs the generator.

docs.title: Task 2.9: ArgoCD Application
docs.text:
Files: - Create: apps/argo-cd-apps/65-llama-cpp.yaml

  • Step 1: Create the Application
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: 65-llama-cpp
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "65"
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: "example.com"
    path: apps/llama-cpp
    targetRevision: HEAD
  destination:
    server: "https://kubernetes.default.svc"
    namespace: default
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true
